question.text: Saraswati Capital Advisors is setting up its maiden Cat II AIF and is debating between offering each HNI a separately managed portfolio versus pooling all contributions into one trust. The Fund Manager, Mr. Ramesh Iyer, argues for pooling. Which of the following is the MOST accurate justification for the pooling approach in the AIF context?

answer.text: Pooling permits the Manager to offer customised, investor-specific decisions at individual corpus level, similar to discretionary PMS
Pooling is mandated by SEBI only for Category III AIFs and is prohibited for Category I and II
Pooling automatically eliminates the need for a PAN at investor level as well as at the fund level under Indian tax law
Pooling creates a blind-pool vehicle enabling economies of scale, broader diversification and collective risk-taking for a common investment objective

explanation.text: The Logic: Chapter 8.1 describes pooling ('blind pool investment') as the foundational principle of AIFs — contributions are pooled into a common corpus managed against a common objective. This enables economies of scale, diversification and enhanced risk-taking capacity, which is the opposite of the customised individual portfolio management (PMS) route. The Trap: Option A describes PMS / individual portfolio management, NOT pooled AIF structure. Option C misstates tax residence rules; pooling only removes PAN-filing at offshore investor level when pooled outside India. Option D is a fabricated rule; pooling is the default for all AIF categories. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (Portfolio Managers) covers the individual corpus / PMS model; XIX-C tests the pooled AIF model as its counterpart. XIX-A/B also reference pooling but from a distributor perspective. Manager's Pro-Tip: When pitching to family offices accustomed to PMS, explain that loss of customisation is the price for economies of scale and access to illiquid deals a single ticket size cannot source — frame pooling as a gateway to opportunity, not a restriction.
